title: Wireshark 101: Your First Packet Analysis
description: Navigate the interface, capture filters, display filters, and follow TCP streams.

slides.title: Wireshark: The Analyst's Microscope 🔬
slides.content:
# The Industry Standard

**Wireshark** is a free, open-source packet analyzer. It lets you **capture** live traffic or **open** saved PCAP files.

**Interface Layout (Default):**
1.  **Packet List Pane (Top):** Summary of each packet (Time, Source, Destination, Protocol, Info).
2.  **Packet Details Pane (Middle):** Drill down into the selected packet's headers (Ethernet -> IP -> TCP -> HTTP).
3.  **Packet Bytes Pane (Bottom):** Raw hexadecimal and ASCII dump of the packet.

**Pro Tip:** You can right-click on any field in the Details Pane and select **'Apply as Column'** to add it to the main view.

slides.title: Capture Filters vs. Display Filters 🎯
slides.content:
# Don't Capture Everything (Unless You Want to Crash)

**Capture Filter (Set BEFORE capturing):** Limits what packets are **saved** to disk.
*   Syntax: **BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter)**
*   *Example:* `host 192.168.1.105 and port 80`
*   *Use Case:* Capturing traffic on a busy server. Only save what you need.

**Display Filter (Set AFTER capturing or opening file):** Limits what packets are **shown** on screen.
*   Syntax: **Wireshark Display Filters**
*   *Example:* `ip.src == 192.168.1.105 && tcp.port == 443`
*   *Use Case:* You have a full PCAP, but you only want to see the suspicious conversation.

**Analogy:** Capture Filter = Choosing which TV channels to **record**. Display Filter = Choosing which part of the recording to **watch**.

quizData.question: You have a 10 GB PCAP file and want to see only traffic involving IP address `10.0.0.5`. Which filter type do you use?
quizData.explanation: Since the file is already captured, you use a Display Filter (`ip.addr == 10.0.0.5`) to view the subset.

slides.title: Essential Display Filters (Memorize These!)
slides.codeSnippet:
# Host / IP Filters
ip.addr == 192.168.1.105          // All traffic to/from this IP
ip.src == 10.0.0.1                // Traffic FROM this IP
ip.dst == 8.8.8.8                 // Traffic TO this IP

# Port Filters
tcp.port == 445                   // All traffic with port 445
tcp.dstport == 3389               // Traffic TO port 3389 (RDP)

# Protocol Filters
http                              // Show only HTTP
http.request                      // Show only HTTP GET/POST requests
dns                               // Show only DNS

# Flag Filters (Advanced)
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0   // SYN packets only (Scans)

slides.title: Follow TCP Stream: The 'Magic' Button ✨
slides.content:
# Reassembling the Conversation

Networks break files into **packets**. Reading them one by one is impossible. Wireshark can **reassemble** the entire conversation.

**How to Use It:**
1.  Right-click on any packet in the conversation.
2.  Select **Follow** -> **TCP Stream**.
3.  A new window opens showing the **entire conversation** in ASCII or Hex.
    *   **Red Text:** Data sent **from** the client.
    *   **Blue Text:** Data sent **from** the server.

**Security Application:**
*   View the **raw HTML** of a phishing page.
*   Extract a **malicious EXE** file transferred over HTTP.
*   See **plaintext passwords** sent over Telnet or FTP.

slides.title: Encryption is the Enemy of PCAP 🔐
slides.content:
## You Can't Follow an Encrypted Stream

If the traffic is **HTTPS (TLS 1.3)** , `Follow TCP Stream` will show **gibberish**. You cannot see the URL path or the file contents.

**Defender Workarounds:**
1.  **SSLKEYLOGFILE:** If you control the endpoint, you can log the session keys and feed them to Wireshark to **decrypt** the traffic.
2.  **JA3/S Fingerprints:** Even if encrypted, the **TLS handshake** reveals the client/server 'fingerprint' (e.g., `Meterpreter` vs `Chrome`). We'll cover this in Lesson 5.
